title: Future continuous and future perfect (continuous)
subtitle: I will be doing / I will have done
summary: Use the future continuous for an activity in progress at a future point, and the future perfect (continuous) for what will be finished - or how long it will have lasted - by then.

lesson.heading: Future continuous: I will be doing
lesson.text: We use the future continuous for something that is predicted to start before a particular point of future time and that may continue after it. It is often the result of a decision or arrangement that has already been made.

examples.text: When it goes into orbit, the spacecraft **will be carrying** 30 kilos of plutonium.
Anna **will be helping** us to organise the party.

lesson.heading: Part of the normal course of events
lesson.text: We also use the future continuous for a future activity that belongs to the normal course of events, or that is one of a repeated or regular series of events.

examples.text: Dr Lin **will be giving** the same talk in room 103 at ten next Thursday.
**Will** you **be driving** to work, as usual?

left.label: Either is possible
left.text: For arranged activities and timetabled events, both forms work.
examples: We **will be leaving** for Istanbul at 7:00 in the evening. (timetabled; or ... **are leaving** ...)

right.label: Future continuous only
right.text: When we are not reporting the details of a programme or timetable, the present continuous is not possible.
examples: When the race starts later this afternoon the drivers **will be hoping** for drier weather than last year. (not ... are hoping ...)

lesson.heading: Keeping willingness out of it
lesson.text: When we don't want to suggest willingness, intention or an invitation, we prefer the future continuous to will. Imagine guests have stayed longer than you wanted and you don't know when they are leaving.

examples.text: **Will you be staying** with us again tonight?
**Will you stay** with us again tonight?
examples.note: they might hear this as an invitation

lesson.heading: Future perfect: I will have done
lesson.text: We use the future perfect to say that something will be ended, completed or achieved by a particular point in the future.

examples.text: By the time you get home I **will have cleaned** the house from top to bottom.
I'm sure his awful behaviour **will** soon **have been forgotten**.

lesson.heading: Future perfect continuous: I will have been doing
lesson.text: We use the future perfect continuous to emphasise the duration of an activity that is in progress at a particular point in the future. With both the future perfect and the future perfect continuous we usually mention the future time.

examples.text: Next year I **will have been working** in the company for 30 years.
**By the time you get home** I will have cleaned the house.
examples.note: the future time is nearly always stated

lesson.heading: Guessing about now - and about the past
lesson.text: All three forms can say what we believe or imagine is happening around now. The future perfect continuous can even say what we think was going on at a point in the past.

examples.text: We could ask to borrow Joe's car. He **won't be using** it today - he went to work by bike.
Most people **will have forgotten** the fire by now.
Tennis fans **will have been queuing** at Wimbledon all day to buy tickets.
Motorist Vicky Hesketh **will have been asking** herself whether speed cameras are a good idea after she was fined 100 pounds last week for driving at 33 mph in a 30 mph zone.

lesson.text: Ask what the sentence says about the future point: still in progress (will be doing), already finished (will have done), or how long it has lasted (will have been doing).

exercises.prompt: Emily writes to a friend in December: 'I suppose by now school ___ for Christmas and you will be enjoying a rest.'
exercises.explanation: 'By now' marks a point by which the closing is complete, so we use the future perfect.

exercises.prompt: We ___ in an hour or so, so make sure your suitcase is packed.
exercises.explanation: An arrangement already made that will be in progress at that future point: will be leaving.

exercises.prompt: Without more cheap housing, families ___ the village and find homes in town.
exercises.explanation: This is a prediction about what people will do, not an arrangement in progress, so will + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: I ___ my car until next week, so you can borrow it if you like.
exercises.explanation: The negative future continuous states a plan without suggesting willingness: won't be using.

exercises.prompt: My grandad ___ a computer. He says he's very happy with his old typewriter.
exercises.explanation: This is about his refusal - his willingness - so we use won't + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Is your suitcase very heavy? I ___ you a hand with it if you like.
exercises.explanation: Offering to do something now takes will + infinitive; the future continuous would remove the offer.

exercises.prompt: Dr Sankey ___ evidence at the trial of James Morgan next week.
exercises.explanation: A future activity that is part of the normal course of events: will be giving.

exercises.prompt: Match each beginning with the ending that completes it.

pairs.left: The weather forecast says that the rain ...
pairs.right: ... will have cleared by the morning and tomorrow will be dry.

pairs.left: If the company is making a profit by the end of the year then we ...
pairs.right: ... will have achieved the objective we set ourselves when we took over.
... will have finished the report before the end of the week.

pairs.left: This book on Proust is really difficult. On Saturday I ...
pairs.right: ... will have been reading it for a month, and I'm still only half way.
... will have been discovering, there have been some late changes to the conference programme.

exercises.prompt: Morneau has been an actor since he was a boy. Say how long his career will have lasted in two years.
exercises.answer: In two years' time Morneau will have been acting for 50 years.
exercises.explanation: The future perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an activity at a future point.

exercises.statement: By the time they get here they will be going to California and New Zealand.
exercises.explanation: By the time they get here they will have been to California and New Zealand. 'By the time ...' needs the future perfect.

exercises.statement: No doubt Joe's children will have been planning it all out for months.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The future perfect continuous can say what we imagine has been going on up to now.

exercises.prompt: Which form does each sentence use?

items.text: My brother Joe and his family will be arriving next Friday.
By now school will have closed for Christmas.
They won't be spending all their time with me.
Most people will have forgotten the fire by now.
Will you be driving to work, as usual?
Next year I will have been working in the company for 30 years.
